title: Sets
body:
A **set** is an unordered collection of distinct things. That is the whole definition, and
the two adjectives are the whole content: order does not matter and duplicates do not
exist. $\{1, 2, 3\}$, $\{3, 1, 2\}$, and $\{1, 2, 2, 3\}$ are the same set.

Sets are the vocabulary layer the rest of the degree assumes without re-teaching it. A
[[Languages|language]] in [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] is *defined* as a set of
[[Strings]] over an [[Alphabet]], so every closure property in that course ("regular
languages are closed under union") is a statement about sets.

## Notation

| Written | Means |
|---|---|
| $x \in A$ | $x$ is an element of $A$ |
| $x \notin A$ | $x$ is not an element of $A$ |
| $\emptyset$ | the empty set, the set with no elements |
| $A \subseteq B$ | every element of $A$ is in $B$ ($A$ is a subset) |
| $A \subset B$ | subset **and** $A \neq B$ (proper subset) |
| $\lvert A \rvert$ | cardinality: how many elements $A$ has |
| $\mathcal{P}(A)$ | power set: the set of all subsets of $A$ |

Two ways to write a set down:

```
roster:       A = {2, 4, 6, 8}
set-builder:  A = { x ∈ ℕ | x is even and x < 10 }
```

Set-builder reads "the set of all $x$ in $\mathbb{N}$ *such that* ...". The bar is "such
that". You use roster notation when the set is small and set-builder when it is infinite,
which in computing is most of the time.

The standard number sets: $\mathbb{N}$ naturals, $\mathbb{Z}$ integers, $\mathbb{Q}$
rationals, $\mathbb{R}$ reals.

## Operations

Given $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$ and $B = \{3, 4\}$ inside a universe $U$:

| Operation | Symbol | Result | Reads as |
|---|---|---|---|
| Union | $A \cup B$ | $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ | in $A$ **or** $B$ |
| Intersection | $A \cap B$ | $\{3\}$ | in $A$ **and** $B$ |
| Difference | $A \setminus B$ | $\{1, 2\}$ | in $A$ but **not** $B$ |
| Complement | $\bar{A}$ | $U \setminus A$ | everything **not** in $A$ |
| Cartesian product | $A \times B$ | $\{(1,3), (1,4), (2,3), \ldots\}$ | all ordered pairs |

Union is or, intersection is and, complement is not. That correspondence is not a
coincidence: it is the same two-element algebra as [[Boolean Algebra]], which is why
De Morgan's laws show up in both places looking identical.

$$\overline{A \cup B} = \bar{A} \cap \bar{B} \qquad \overline{A \cap B} = \bar{A} \cup \bar{B}$$

The Cartesian product is the odd one out: its elements are **ordered pairs**, so order
suddenly does matter again inside them. $\lvert A \times B \rvert = \lvert A \rvert \times \lvert B \rvert$.

## Counting

- $\lvert A \cup B \rvert = \lvert A \rvert + \lvert B \rvert - \lvert A \cap B \rvert$.
  This is **inclusion-exclusion**: add both, then subtract the overlap you counted twice.
- A set with $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets. Each element is either in or out, which is $n$
  independent binary choices, which is the same argument as why $n$ bits give $2^n$ values
  in [[Boolean Representation]].
- The empty set is a subset of every set, including itself.
- $\emptyset$ and $\{\emptyset\}$ are different: the first has no elements, the second has
  one element (which happens to be empty).

## Proving two sets equal

The standard move, and the one worth memorising, because it turns a set claim into two
[[Direct Proof]]s:

> To show $A = B$, show $A \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq A$.

And to show $A \subseteq B$: take an arbitrary $x \in A$, and argue that $x \in B$. The
word "arbitrary" is doing the work. You picked no particular $x$, so the argument covers
all of them.

```
Claim: A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C)

(⊆)  Let x ∈ A ∩ (B ∪ C).
     Then x ∈ A, and x ∈ B or x ∈ C.
     Case x ∈ B:  x ∈ A ∩ B, so x ∈ (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C).
     Case x ∈ C:  x ∈ A ∩ C, so x ∈ (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C).

(⊇)  Let x ∈ (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C).  ... same idea, run backwards.

Both inclusions hold, so the sets are equal. ∎
```

## Where this is used

- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]]: [[Languages]] are sets of [[Strings]]. Union,
  intersection, and complement of languages are exactly these operations, and "closed
  under" means the result is still in the same class.
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]]: a [[Graph]] is a pair of sets, $V$ and $E$. [[Maps]] and
  [[Hashing]] implement a set with fast membership testing, which is the $x \in A$ question
  made into a data structure.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]]: sets are the vocabulary the type and
  [[Data Structure]] discussions borrow.
- [[Permutation]] and [[Combination]] count subsets and arrangements *of* a set.
- [[STATISTICS]] (MATH 2234): **an event is a set and the probability axioms are stated on
  sets.** Union is "or", intersection is "and", complement is $1 - P$, disjoint is mutually
  exclusive, and inclusion-exclusion is $P(A \cup B) = P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$. Venn diagrams in
  that course are this note's material; see [[Probability]].

## Not covered in the vault

Relations, functions as sets of ordered pairs, equivalence classes, and countability
(the $\lvert \mathbb{N} \rvert$ versus $\lvert \mathbb{R} \rvert$ argument) have no notes
anywhere. The last one matters for [[Undecidability]], which uses diagonalisation without
this course having introduced it.
